 Campground prepares for more danger after Four Corners flood damage
 By Savannah Eller 
 Published October 30, 2026 6:53pm 
 | 
 Updated October 30, 2026 7:12pm 
 + 
 Add The Gazette on Google
 Tiny homes at Fun Valley Family Resort were swept away by flooding that hit the Four Corners region last week. (Courtesy of Kathy Smith) 
 When Kathy Smith was allowed past a roadblock to check on Fun Valley Family Resort near South Fork late last week, the Rio Grande that winds through it wasn’t where it ought to be.
 “It’s been flowing through the Aspen RV sites. It’s still flowing through there,” she said Thursday evening.

 With more rain and a chance of flooding in the forecast this weekend, Smith and her husband Mike were doing their best to wrangle water away from the buildings that remain intact on the sprawling resort property first opened in 1959. The Smiths are Texas residents who run Fun Valley as general managers. The resort is closed for the season, so no visitors were present.
 “We’re just trying to protect what we have,” Smith said. 
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 The damage from last week’s storm was already devastating. Debris had clogged a bridge over the river, forcing water around it. Some of the resort’s row of red-roofed tiny homes were pushed over each other like dominoes. Elsewhere, large ravel trailers were similarly crushed into a pile by the force of the water.
 Flood damage at Fun Valley Family Resort. (Courtesy of Kathy Smith) 
 The resort is one of hundreds of properties affected by the flood, which began last Wednesday as what remained of Hurricane Trudy dissipated far inland. Communities like Pagosa Springs saw major flood damage. In Archuleta County to the south, many roads remained impassable days later.
 The storm was deadly in other areas of the Four Corners region, which includes Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Arizona. People in the path were evacuated, and hundreds required rescues.
 It’s not the first storm to hit the region in a fall that brought saturating rains. The latest weather reports indicate it won’t be the last. In a Facebook post Friday afternoon, the Archuleta County Sheriff’s Office advised any residents in low-lying areas to evacuate ahead of more precipitation.
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 “If you have water on your property now, expect more with this storm,” the post read. 
 The south fork of the Rio Grande, in a normal year, is a tame and beloved feature of Fun Valley, where Smith said children get a certificate for catching their first fish. Flows on the river were low this summer, impacted by regional drought and historically low snowpack. The tubing operation suffered.
 Things turn around drastically when the rain comes. Last year, flooding on the river impacted Pagosa Springs downstream but largely missed the resort. The Rio Grande peaked at about 3,000 cubic feet per second at Fun Valley, said Smith.
 “We kept saying we were really and truly lucky last year,” she said. 
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 As the storm hit last week, the Smiths watched remotely from security cameras. One at the riverbank showed a “tubes exit here” sign. When the sign disappeared underwater, Smith said she knew there was trouble. 
 The river crested in the evening last Friday at 7,000 cubic feet per second, according to Smith. 
 “There’s nothing you can do about it,” she said. 
 The campground and RV park with its own grocery store, restaurant and gift shop has about 100 employees. It hasn’t seen a major flood since its creation. Smith said people come back to visit Fun Valley year after year, while employees range from retirees to college students. 
 ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT 
 “We don’t have all the answers yet,” she said.
